items.editor_note: Applies f-divergence self-play with LLMs to mixed-type tabular anomaly detection.

items.title: PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models
items.summary_1line: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about an...
items.editor_note: Consensus decoding against cross-modal hallucination in omnimodal models.

items.title: On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents
items.summary_1line: User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably d...

items.title: Jailbreak Detection on Large Language Models via Contrastive Prototype Structures
items.summary_1line: Jailbreak attempts and harmful prompts remain a challenge for the safe deployment of large language models. We study whether contrastively learned representations can support safety detection without training an addit...
items.editor_note: Detects jailbreaks from contrastive representations without a separate classifier.

items.title: Measuring Hallucination in Large Language Models for Cyber Threat Intelligence: An Exploratory Study
items.summary_1line: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in cyber threat intelligence (CTI) tasks, such as summarization and question answering. However, they may produce hallucinations, false or misleading content not grounded in the source text, which can mislead analysts and corrupt
items.editor_note: Measures hallucination in cyber threat intelligence summarization and QA.

items.title: The Geometry of Lies: Knowledge and Persona Directions for Detecting Deception in Large Language Models
items.summary_1line: Linear probes are the cheapest LLM lie detectors but often fail to transfer across kinds of lie. items.editor_note: Tests label-free lie-detection directions at 70B scale, including lies about knowledge.

items.title: Evaluating Prompting Strategies for Zero-Shot Multilingual Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis with Large Language Models
items.summary_1line: Evaluates zero-shot multilingual aspect-based sentiment triplet extraction across 12 languages, three domains and seven open-weight LLMs under four prompting strategies, finding direct monolithic prompting performs best.

items.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
items.summary_1line: MemOnce proposes an LLM architecture that caches compact final-layer hidden states as memory and decodes them into KV caches, reporting a 1313× smaller memory state cache and 6.9× lower prefill latency for Qwen3.5-4B at 1M context.
items.editor_note: Reports 1313x smaller memory cache and 6.9x lower prefill latency at 1M context.

items.title: Population-Based Post-Training for Large Language Models
items.summary_1line: Introduces Population-Based Post-Training (PBPT), which trains several RLVR models in parallel and uses population-based training to tune hyperparameters, reporting stronger agents than compute-matched independent runs on four benchmarks.
items.editor_note: Population-based hyperparameter tuning across parallel RLVR runs beats compute-matched baselines.

items.title: Training-Free Interventions for Hallucination in Large Language Models
items.summary_1line: A survey of 116 works on inference-time methods for reducing LLM hallucination, comparing intervention families by evidence source, model access, and preparation cost, and noting metrics and limits to reported gains.
items.editor_note: Surveys 116 inference-time hallucination methods and flags limits on reported gains.

items.title: mini-psych-agent: Evaluating Human-Like Behavior in LLM Agents through Interactive Psychological Environments
items.summary_1line: Presents mini-psych-agent, which converts psychological tasks into interactive environments and uses a learned human-policy model to measure how closely LLM agents' behavior matches human choices, finding this varies with agent configuration and task.
items.why_it_matters: Matches feed focus: agentic, harness, evaluation.
items.editor_note: Measures how closely LLM agents match human choices in psychological tasks.

items.title: Rethinking the Evaluation of Contrastive Decoding for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.summary_1line: Introduces CONCOR, a controlled benchmark that scores how contrastive decoding methods rank ground-truth objects against hallucinated candidates in multimodal LLMs, using a Contrastive Grounding Margin metric.
items.editor_note: CONCOR benchmark re-scores contrastive decoding for multimodal hallucination.

items.title: Test-Time Latent Computation to Improve Visual Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.summary_1line: Proposes Lobals, a training-free decoding method that re-runs a contiguous window of MLLM layers with the strongest visual-token attention to revisit visual evidence, reporting gains on vision-language, hallucination, and vision-centric tasks.
items.editor_note: Training-free layer re-run that revisits visual evidence in multimodal models.

items.title: ReQOR: Operator-Discrepancy Subspace Repair for Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors in Large Language Models
items.summary_1line: Proposes ReQOR, a training-free defense against quantization-conditioned backdoors in LLMs that repairs dominant same-state operator discrepancies on benign calibration data via a factorized residual adapter, tested on four LLMs.
items.editor_note: Training-free repair for backdoors that activate only after quantization, tested on four LLMs.

items.title: Joint Estimation of Abilities and Item Parameters for Large Language Models Using Probability and Binary Responses: A Fractional-Response IRT Framework
items.summary_1line: Large language model (LLM) evaluations provide two response types: probabilities assigned to correct answers and binary indicators of correctness. Restricting evaluation to one type narrows the range of available models or discards probability information. We propose a method to
items.editor_note: IRT framework that uses both probability and correctness responses in one eval.

items.title: Interactive Proofs as a Unified Framework for Evaluating and Leveraging Verifiable Proof Generation by LLM Agents
items.summary_1line: Introduces Merlin-Bench, a benchmark of 100 cases across 15 problem families that tests whether LLM agents can produce proofs a formal verifier accepts under interactive-proof protocols, and reports that 10 frontier LLMs struggle with this.
items.why_it_matters: Matches feed focus: agent, harness, eval.
items.editor_note: 100 verifier-checked proof cases; 10 frontier LLMs struggle.

items.title: VulnSafe: Measuring Vulnerability-Aware Relational Safety in Large Language Models
items.summary_1line: VulnSafe is a Chinese benchmark that scores LLMs on five relational safety constructs across 41 scenarios and 2,050 prompts, finding distinct competence profiles across eight models and larger gaps on proactive than prohibitive behavior.
items.editor_note: 2,050 Chinese prompts show larger gaps on proactive than prohibitive safety behavior.

editorial.tldr: This slug used to track speculative decoding; after reclustering it holds 35 unrelated arXiv papers from Nov 9 onward whose only link is "Large Language Models" in the title. Read it as a research digest: most papers question how LLMs are evaluated, measure hallucination and uncertainty, or probe safety, with a few on infra such as LM-SimBench and MemOnce.
editorial.whats_new: Two more benchmarks landed Nov 25: Merlin-Bench finds 10 frontier LLMs struggle to produce proofs a formal verifier accepts, and VulnSafe scores eight models on 2,050 Chinese relational-safety prompts.
editorial.why_it_matters: There is no single event here. The useful signal is that eval methodology itself keeps getting challenged (shifting human raters, adaptive users, unvalidated user simulators), which is the layer your agent eval harness depends on.
editorial.take_for_builders: If your agent evals rely on a user simulator or LLM-as-judge, validate it against a small human-labeled set before trusting a week-over-week regression signal.

beats.headline: LLMs applied to AutoML, fault diagnosis, anomaly detection and program induction
beats.summary: Domain papers that use an LLM as a component; little here touches serving or agent infrastructure.

beats.headline: Papers question whether LLM evaluations measure what they claim
beats.summary: Human raters getting stricter, users adapting mid-conversation, unvalidated user simulators and name-only knowledge probes each can skew a score.

beats.headline: Uncertainty, abstention and decoding-time fixes for hallucination
beats.summary: Black-box uncertainty estimates, calibrated abstention thresholds, deception probes, and training-free multimodal decoding fixes, capped by a 116-paper survey.

beats.headline: Framing attacks, jailbreak detection, malware triage and quantization backdoors
beats.summary: Security-side papers: how headline framing sways model judgments, detecting jailbreaks without an extra classifier, and repairing backdoors that only fire after quantization.

beats.headline: Training simulators, memory-compressed long context and population-based RL
beats.summary: The platform-relevant slice: LM-SimBench for parallelism simulators, a survey of LLMs for AI infra, MemOnce's compact KV memory, and RL post-training methods for agents.

beats.headline: Merlin-Bench and VulnSafe add verifier-checked proofs and relational safety

open_questions: Does MemOnce's reported 1313x smaller memory cache at 1M context hold up in an independent reproduction or open serving stack?
Do other labs adopt Merlin-Bench's verifier-checked proof protocol for agent evals?
Does the "raters got pickier" finding change how ChatGPT-style regressions are reported or re-tested?
Will reclustering pull speculative-decoding papers back into this slug, or does it stay a generic LLM-research grab-bag?
